description: We’re a team of developers and IT engineers from Ukraine who love science, our planet, ecology, and music. We also have a very talented musician, so we want to turn Earth data into something you can hear.
summary:
Earth Jukebox turns NASA Earth imagery and live weather into music you can explore by ear. It was built for people who are blind or have low vision, and for everyone who learns better by listening. 
Earth science is almost always shown as maps and colour scales, so those people are left out. Our web app reads a NASA aerosol visualization from the Earth Information Center (SVS 5669) pixel by pixel and plays it as a four-voice score: time runs west to east, the north sings higher, and more colour plays louder. A second side plays the planet's current weather every 30 minutes over a NASA GIBS Blue Marble map. 
This answers the challenge directly: an Earth Information Jukebox where you pick a record, press Play and hear what NASA sees. 
Everything works with a screen reader and a keyboard, in English and Ukrainian, and every sound can be exported as data so anyone can check it.
details:
What it does.
Earth Jukebox is a web app that plays Earth data as music. The home screen is a shelf of records in two rows:

  • NASA archive: Create your mix, Four aerosols, Gentle scale, Quick tour.
    https://earth-jukebox-693055241155.europe-west1.run.app/?p=nasa-quick
  • Live: Create your mix, Rain right now, Heat and cold, Wind map, Clouds, AI composes.
    https://earth-jukebox-693055241155.europe-west1.run.app/?p=live-rain

Press Play and a playhead moves across the world map while you listen. Hover or tap any point of the map to hear that place and have it read out. "Create your mix" opens sound settings where you choose the layers, density, length and musical mode yourself.


How it works.

  • NASA archive. The frame of NASA SVS 5669 (GEOS aerosols, 19 Aug 2025, 20:00 UTC, GEOS-FP 2 km Replay by NASA GMAO) is split into the four legend layers by colour: black carbon, dust, sea salt and sulfate. The map is cut into 128 columns from west to east. For each column and layer we measure the area it covers (corrected for latitude) and where its main band sits. Longitude becomes time, area becomes loudness, latitude becomes pitch, and each aerosol gets its own instrument. The result is fitted to a scale or a slow chord progression and rendered as five WAV stems plus MIDI.
  • Live. Current temperature, precipitation, cloud cover and wind on a 10° grid (648 points) refresh every 30 minutes. A sine wave crosses the planet and the weather under it becomes a score for 6–7 instruments. The northern hemisphere plays in the left ear and the southern in the right. A rule-based composer writes the score by default. An optional AI composer can write the same score format, and every score is checked before it plays.

For more details: https://earth-jukebox-693055241155.europe-west1.run.app/how

Benefits.

  • Built for blind and low-vision users first: screen reader support, full keyboard control, spoken narration, sound captions, high contrast, colour-blind palettes, vibration, a tactile map export, English and Ukrainian.
  • Honest and testable: the same input always gives the same notes, and every piece can be exported as CSV, JSON, MIDI, WAV, captions (VTT) and text, so a scientist or a teacher can check what the sound means.
  • Free and open source (MIT). It runs anywhere with one command, no keys needed.

What we want to achieve. Make Earth science something you can hear, not only see. Next steps: more Earth Information Center frames played through time, real model values instead of colour area, sessions with blind listeners, and kits for museums and classrooms.

Technologies.

  • Programming languages: TypeScript, C#, Python.
  • Software:
    Frontend: React 19 and Vite
    API: ASP.NET Core on .NET 10
    Sound Service: FastAPI with NumPy and Pillow
    Deploy: Docker Compose and nginx
    Testing: Tested with Vitest, Testing Library, axe-core, pytest and xUnit
  • Hardware: any laptop that runs Docker to host it, and any modern browser on a desktop or phone to use it. Headphones are recommended to hear the north/south stereo mapping. No special hardware.
